e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Giovanni, the Italian form of John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. Spellings in Jo- are especially common among Hispanic families in the US.

assoc.t: Jovani, a prom and evening gown label

e.etymology: From Arabic arham, most merciful, from the root of rahma, mercy; in the Quran God is called the most merciful of the merciful. It is especially popular among South Asian Muslims.

A modern respelling of Bentley, an English place name and surname from Old English beonet, bent grass, and leah, clearing. Bentley took off as a first name after a baby on MTV's 16 and Pregnant in 2009.

assoc.t: Bentley, the British luxury car maker

e.etymology: From Hawaiian ka leo, the voice or the sound. It is also a short form of longer Hawaiian names that begin the same way.

assoc.t: Kaleo, the Icelandic rock band behind Way Down We Go

e.etymology: The Latin form of Odysseus, the wily Greek hero of Homer's Odyssey. Americans took it up in the 1800s, and it peaked in the 1880s in honor of the general and president Ulysses S. Grant.
namesakes: Ulysses S. Grant (Civil War general and 18th US president)
Ulysses (Roman name for Odysseus, hero of Homer's Odyssey)

assoc.t: Ulysses S. Grant, Union general and 18th president
Ulysses, the Roman name of Odysseus in the Odyssey
Ulysses, James Joyce's 1922 novel

e.etymology: From Sanskrit amara, undying or immortal. The same spelling serves for the Arabic name Ammar, long-lived, which is common in Bosnia, and amar is the Spanish verb to love.

From Greek Akhilleus, the greatest warrior of the Trojan War and hero of Homer's Iliad; later legend made his heel his one weak spot. The meaning is uncertain; an old tradition links it to akhos, grief.
namesakes: Achilles (hero of Homer's Iliad, played by Brad Pitt in Troy)

assoc.t: Greek hero of the Trojan War in Homer's Iliad
Achilles' heel, a fatal weakness, and the Achilles tendon

e.note: Calls up the phrase Achilles' heel and the Achilles tendon, so expect weak-spot jokes.

e.etymology: The Scandinavian spelling of Matthias, the Greek form of Hebrew Mattityahu, gift of Yahweh. Matthias is the apostle chosen to replace Judas; Matthew is the same name.
From Arabic rami, archer or one who throws. In Finland the same spelling is a pet form of Abraham and Raimo.
namesakes: Rami Malek (Oscar-winning star of Bohemian Rhapsody and Mr. Robot)

e.etymology: From the Old French form of Hieronymus, Greek hieros, sacred, and onoma, name. Saint Jerome translated the Bible into Latin around the year 400.
namesakes: Saint Jerome (scholar who translated the Bible into Latin)
Jerome Powell (Federal Reserve chair from 2018)
Jerome Bettis (Hall of Fame Steelers running back)

e.etymology: First recorded in England in the 1600s. It may come from Latin Caelina, heavenly, or be a form of Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon; Selena is the same name.
namesakes: Selina Kyle (Catwoman's real name in the Batman stories)
Selina Meyer (Julia Louis-Dreyfus's character on Veep)

assoc.t: Selina Kyle, Catwoman's real name in Batman
sounds like Selena, the late Tejano star, and Selena Gomez

e.etymology: From Arabic rayyan, well-watered or lush, built on rayy, watering. In Islamic tradition Ar-Rayyan is the gate of Paradise reserved for those who fast.
e.note: Often misread as Ryan, a different name.

e.etymology: A nickname for Sigmund, Zygmunt and similar names. David Bowie's 1972 alter ego Ziggy Stardust and the reggae singer Ziggy Marley made it familiar as a name of its own.
namesakes: Ziggy Marley (reggae musician, son of Bob Marley)
Ziggy Stardust (David Bowie's glam-rock stage persona)

assoc.t: Ziggy Stardust, David Bowie's glam-rock alter ego
Ziggy Marley, reggae singer and son of Bob Marley
Ziggy, the luckless hero of the newspaper comic strip

e.etymology: From Hebrew adi, ornament, and el, God. The name appears in the Old Testament book of Chronicles, and today it is used in Israel and by Spanish-speaking families.
The Spanish and Portuguese spelling of Rebecca, from Hebrew Rivka, the wife of Isaac in Genesis. The Hebrew is usually tied to a word for a snare or a tie, read as captivating.
A modern Indian girls' name, popular with Hindu families in India and abroad. Name lists gloss it as beloved or gift of God, but its Sanskrit derivation is not well documented.
In the US mostly a spelling of Raylee, a blend of Ray or Rae and the -leigh ending. Rayleigh is also an English surname and a town in Essex, of the same origin as Raleigh.

assoc.t: Rayleigh scattering, the physics of why the sky is blue

e.etymology: A spelling of Sunny, the English word for bright and cheerful, long a nickname and now given as a full name. It is rising along with Goldie, Birdie and other nickname-style names.
e.note: Sounds the same as the boys' name Sonny and close to Sunni, the largest branch of Islam.

e.etymology: The French elaboration of Angèle, from Greek angelos, messenger, the word that became angel. Angelina is its sister form. It was most popular in the US around 1915.
A short form of Elizabeth, from Hebrew Elisheva, my God is an oath, the name of the mother of John the Baptist. Liz is also used for Lisa, Eliza and Lizbeth.
namesakes: Liz Taylor (Elizabeth Taylor, Hollywood star of Cleopatra)
Liz Cheney (former Wyoming congresswoman)
Liz Lemon (Tina Fey's character on 30 Rock)

e.etymology: From Arabic iman, faith or belief, a central term in Islam. It is given to both girls and boys, and the Somali-born supermodel Iman made it familiar in the US.
namesakes: Iman (Somali-American supermodel, widow of David Bowie)
Iman Shumpert (NBA champion and Dancing with the Stars winner)

assoc.t: Iman, the Somali-American supermodel

e.etymology: From the Himalayan region divided between India and Pakistan, whose goats gave cashmere wool its name. As an American boys' name it rose in the 2010s alongside Kash and Cash.

assoc.t: Himalayan region contested by India and Pakistan
Kashmir, Led Zeppelin's 1975 rock epic
sounds like cashmere, the soft wool named for the region

e.note: The region is known for a long and sometimes violent territorial dispute.

e.etymology: The English word for a sacred song, from Greek psalmos, a song sung to a harp. Kim Kardashian and Kanye West brought it attention as a name when they chose it for their son in 2019.

assoc.t: the Psalms, the Bible's book of sacred songs

e.note: The P is silent, and said aloud the name is easily heard as Sam.

e.etymology: A spelling of Leslie, a Scottish surname from a place in Aberdeenshire, in Gaelic lios cuileann, garden of hollies. This spelling is a favorite of Hispanic families in the US.
A spelling of Kamari, a modern American name in the family of Jamari, Amari and Omari. The Kh- opening follows names such as Khalil.
From Hebrew Shoshannah, lily, through the Greek of the Bible. Susanna is a virtuous woman falsely accused in the Book of Daniel and a follower of Jesus in Luke; Susan is its short form.
namesakes: Susanna Hoffs (lead singer of the Bangles)

assoc.t: Oh! Susanna, Stephen Foster's 1848 folk song

e.etymology: An English surname of uncertain origin. Americans first gave it as a first name in honor of the 19th-century preacher William Ellery Channing; the actor Channing Tatum revived it around 2010.
namesakes: Channing Tatum (star of Magic Mike and 21 Jump Street)

assoc.t: actor Channing Tatum

e.etymology: From Arabic saniyya, radiant or brilliant. In the US it took off in the 2000s with the sound-alike names Aniyah, Janiyah and Taniyah.
A spelling of Rylan, a modern name shaped from the English surname Ryland, land where rye is grown, with the sound of Ryan and Dylan.
A short form of Augustus or August, Latin for venerable, and of Gustav and Angus. Greek Americans also use it for Kostas, short for Konstantinos.
namesakes: Gus Grissom (Mercury astronaut who died in the Apollo 1 fire)
Gus Van Sant (director of Good Will Hunting)
Gus Fring (drug kingpin in Breaking Bad)

assoc.t: Gus Fring, the fast-food drug lord of Breaking Bad
Gus, the plump mouse in Disney's Cinderella

e.etymology: From the bright, daisy-like garden flower, native to Mexico, which Linnaeus named for the German botanist Johann Gottfried Zinn.

assoc.t: zinnia, a bright summer garden flower

e.etymology: A blend of Emma and the -lynn ending, or a respelling of the older name Emmeline.
